+++ question | Adding two signed bytes
--- ask
An 8-bit ALU adds 0x64 (100) and 0x32 (50). Which flags does it set? (N: negative, Z: zero, C: carry out, V: signed overflow.)
--- choice
C = 1 and V = 0, because 150 does not fit in a byte.
--- choice correct
N = 1, C = 0 and V = 1: the result 0x96 is 150 unsigned but reads as −106 signed.
--- choice
No flags: 150 fits in 8 bits, so nothing went wrong.
--- why
100 + 50 = 150 = 0x96 fits in 8 unsigned bits, so there is no carry out. But as a signed byte 0x96 is −106: two positive numbers gave a negative result, which is signed overflow, and its top bit sets N. Carry is about unsigned overflow and V about signed overflow; they are independent.

+++ question | Floats between one and two
--- ask
How many different single-precision floats x satisfy 1 ≤ x < 2? Type a number.
--- answer
8388608
8,388,608
2^23
2**23
--- why
Every float in [1, 2) has exponent field 127 and differs only in its 23 fraction bits, so there are 2²³ = 8,388,608 of them, evenly spaced 2⁻²³ apart. Each power-of-two interval holds the same number of floats, which is why their spacing doubles from one interval to the next.

+++ question | Why NAND is enough
--- ask
Which reason shows that every Boolean function can be built from NAND gates alone?
--- choice
NAND has the most transistors of any gate, so it can do the most.
--- choice correct
NOT a is NAND(a, a), AND is NOT of NAND, and OR follows by De Morgan; with NOT, AND and OR, any truth table can be written as an OR of ANDs.
--- choice
Every gate in a real chip is secretly a NAND gate.
--- why
Any truth table is an OR of one AND term per row where the output is 1 (the sum-of-products form). NAND gives NOT (tie the inputs), AND (NAND then NOT) and OR (NAND of the two inverted inputs, by De Morgan). So NAND builds all three, and therefore everything.

+++ question | Why a register file needs an edge
--- ask
A register's D input is fed from its own output plus one, through an adder. Why must the register be edge-triggered rather than a transparent latch?
--- choice
A latch cannot hold more than one bit.
--- choice correct
While a latch is transparent, its new output flows through the adder and back into it, so the value would race upward uncontrollably; an edge-triggered flip-flop takes one new value per clock edge.
--- choice
An adder cannot drive a latch's input.
--- why
A transparent latch passes changes through for the whole time its enable is on, so a loop through it keeps recomputing: the count would depend on gate delays. A flip-flop samples its input only at the rising edge and holds its output steady for the whole cycle, so each cycle adds exactly one.

+++ question | The furthest a branch reaches
--- ask
An RV32I conditional branch encodes a 13-bit signed byte offset whose lowest bit is always 0. What is the largest forward offset, in bytes, that it can reach? Type a number.
--- answer
4094
--- why
A 13-bit two's complement number runs from −4096 to +4095; the lowest bit is always 0 (instructions are at least 2-byte aligned), so the largest even value is 4094. With 4-byte instructions the furthest real target is 4092 bytes ahead.

+++ question | The function that loses its way home
--- ask
Which change fixes this RISC-V function, which calls `helper` and then returns?

```text
work:  addi sp, sp, -16
       jal  ra, helper
       addi a0, a0, 1
       addi sp, sp, 16
       jr   ra
```
--- choice
Replace `jr ra` with `jal ra, work`.
--- choice correct
Save ra on the stack before the call (`sw ra, 12(sp)`) and load it back before `jr ra` (`lw ra, 12(sp)`).
--- choice
Remove the stack adjustments, since the function stores nothing.
--- why
`jal ra, helper` overwrites ra with the address after the call, so `jr ra` jumps back into `work` itself, forever, instead of to work's caller. ra is caller-saved: a function that makes a call must keep its own return address in its stack frame across that call.

+++ question | Control signals for a store
--- ask
In the single-cycle datapath, which control settings does `sw` need?
--- choice
RegWrite = 1, MemWrite = 1, and the ALU adds two registers.
--- choice correct
RegWrite = 0, MemWrite = 1, and the ALU adds the base register and the sign-extended immediate.
--- choice
RegWrite = 0, MemRead = 1, and the ALU compares the two registers.
--- why
A store writes memory, not a register, so RegWrite is 0 and MemWrite is 1. The address is base + offset, so the ALU's second input comes from the S-type immediate, not from rs2; rs2 carries the value to store to the memory's data input.

+++ question | Cycles on the pipeline
--- ask
The lesson's five-stage pipeline with forwarding runs 10 instructions. Exactly one load is immediately followed by an instruction that uses its result, and exactly one branch in the middle is taken. How many cycles does it take? Type a number.
--- answer
17
--- why
With forwarding the total is n + 4 + L + 2T: 10 instructions, 4 more cycles to drain the pipeline, 1 load-use stall and 2 cycles for the taken branch: 10 + 4 + 1 + 2 = 17.

+++ question | A partial speedup
--- ask
A new vector unit makes 40% of a program's run time 4 times faster and leaves the rest unchanged. What is the overall speedup, to two decimal places?
--- choice
1.60
--- choice correct
1.43
--- choice
4.00
--- why
By Amdahl's law the new time is 0.6 + 0.4 / 4 = 0.7 of the old, so the speedup is 1 / 0.7 ≈ 1.43. The untouched 60% dominates: even an infinitely fast vector unit would give only 1 / 0.6 ≈ 1.67.

+++ question | Index bits of a set-associative cache
--- ask
A cache holds 64 KiB in 64-byte blocks and is 4-way set-associative. How many bits of the address select the set? Type a number.
--- answer
8
--- why
64 KiB / 64 B = 1,024 lines; in sets of 4 ways that is 256 sets, and 256 = 2⁸ needs 8 index bits. (A direct-mapped cache of the same size would need 10.)

+++ question | Which loop order
--- ask
For C = A × B with row-major n × n matrices too big for the cache, which innermost loop gives the fewest misses per iteration?
--- choice
The loop over i, because it is the outermost index of C.
--- choice correct
The loop over j, because then B[k][j] and C[i][j] are walked along rows with stride 1 and A[i][k] stays fixed.
--- choice
The loop over k, because then C[i][j] stays fixed in a register.
--- why
With j innermost (orders ikj and kij), two of the three arrays move with stride 1, costing a miss every few iterations, and the third is fixed: about 0.5 misses per iteration with 4 elements per block. With k innermost, B is walked down a column (1.25), and with i innermost, A and C both are (2).

+++ question | Why a DMA transfer needs the cache's attention
--- ask
A camera writes a new image into memory by DMA. Right afterwards, the processor reads the image and sometimes sees parts of the previous one. Why?
--- choice
DMA writes are slower than the processor's reads, so the image is not finished yet.
--- choice correct
The processor's cache still holds blocks of the old image at those addresses; the device wrote memory, not the cache, so the stale blocks must be invalidated.
--- choice
The TLB still translates the image's addresses to the old frames.
--- why
DMA moves data between the device and memory without going through the processor's cache. Any cached copies of those addresses are now stale, and reads hit them. Drivers invalidate those blocks after the transfer (and write back dirty ones before a device reads memory), unless the hardware keeps DMA coherent.
